title: The Shared Dream - An Overview / Review
body:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HlwfZ6atyLw

Daniel (@dungeondive) bought The Shared Dream and every expansion he could find on first impressions, and two plays later he isn't sure he loves it. It's a horror threat-management game ("Pandemic meets Arkham Horror 2nd edition") based on the RPG Of Dreams and Magic. A friend had asked him for horror games that aren't Cthulhu, and that is what drew him in.

His biggest complaint is the look. A thematic game must either look great or have a bold, distinctive style, and he thinks this one has neither: mismatched iconography, a scenario card in Comic Sans, placeholder-looking art. On the table it looks like three or four games' components mixed together. He makes a plea to designers to check Urban Dictionary before naming their threat tokens "taint."

He likes the tension between Conviction and Nightmare. Every hero has a waking self and a dream Animus, and summoning the Animus feeds the nightmare that spawns enemies. He also likes the Echoes deck. The scenario stories, though, run on rails, so they will lose their surprise on replay. Two-hero play only shrinks the map. Enemies don't scale, and a boss with six movement against heroes with two can turn a game into a string of twenty rolls you have to win. He's keeping it, mostly for the solo Crux Collection.

----

Daniel admits the art is a big reason he can't get into The Shared Dream. How much does a game's visual coherence decide whether you stay engaged with it?
